cards: Alexander the Great, Alexander III of Macedon, was king of Macedon from 336 to 323 BCE.
Philip II was king of Macedon from 359 to 336 BCE and the father of Alexander the Great.
Aristotle was a Greek philosopher of the fourth century BCE whose works covered logic, ethics, politics and natural science.
Plato was an Athenian philosopher of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, author of dialogues such as the Republic.
Ptolemy I Soter was a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who became ruler of Egypt after Alexander's death.
Mencius (Mengzi) was a Confucian philosopher of the 4th century BCE, born in the State of Zou in Shandong.
Chandragupta Maurya was the founder of the Maurya Empire, which he established in 321 BCE after overthrowing the Nanda dynasty, traditionally with the help of Chanakya.
founded empire 321 BCE · South & Southeast Asia
Dionysius I was tyrant of Syracuse from 405 to 367 BCE and the most powerful Greek ruler in the west of his time.
Demetrius I, called Poliorcetes, 'the Besieger', was a Macedonian general, son of Antigonus I.
Agesilaus II was king of Sparta from about 400 to 360 BCE, during the period of Spartan supremacy after the Peloponnesian War.
Demosthenes was an Athenian statesman and the greatest orator of ancient Greece.
Epaminondas was a Theban general and statesman who, with Pelopidas, made Thebes the leading power of Greece.
Perdiccas was a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who became regent of the empire after Alexander's death in 323 BCE.
Zhuangzi (Zhuang Zhou) was a Daoist philosopher of the 4th century BCE, a native of the State of Song.
Antipater was a Macedonian general and statesman who served Philip II and governed Macedon and Greece while Alexander the Great campaigned in Asia.
Chanakya, also known as Kautilya, was an ancient Indian scholar and statesman traditionally regarded as the chief adviser to Chandragupta Maurya.
Agathocles of Syracuse seized power as tyrant of Syracuse in 317 BCE and later took the title of king.
Demetrius of Phalerum was an Athenian statesman and Peripatetic philosopher, a pupil of Theophrastus.
Mausolus was the Hecatomnid ruler of Caria from 377 to 353 BCE, formally a Persian satrap but in practice an independent dynast.
Artaxerxes III was an Achaemenid king who reigned from 358 BCE until he was assassinated in 338 BCE.
Pelopidas was a Theban general and statesman who led the exiles who freed Thebes from its Spartan garrison in 379 BCE.
Mahapadma Nanda was the founder of the Nanda dynasty of Magadha, who around 345 BCE overthrew the last Shishunaga king.
Marcus Furius Camillus was a Roman statesman and general of the early fourth century BCE.
Seuthes III was a king of the Odrysian Kingdom in Thrace in the late 4th century BCE.
Shang Yang was a Chinese statesman and Legalist thinker, a nobleman of the State of Wey, who served Duke Xiao of Qin from 361 BCE.
Iphicrates was an Athenian general known for his use of light-armed peltasts, with which he destroyed a Spartan regiment near Corinth around 390 BCE.
Qu Yuan (c. 340–278 BCE) was a poet and minister of the State of Chu, traditionally regarded as the first great individual poet of China.
Aeschines was an Athenian orator and statesman, the chief political opponent of Demosthenes.
Alexander I of Epirus, called the Molossian, was king of the Molossians in Epirus and the brother-in-law and uncle of Alexander the Great.
Herophilus of Chalcedon was a Greek physician who worked in Alexandria under the early Ptolemies and is often called the father of anatomy.
c. 335 – c. 280 BCE · Egypt & North Africa
Herostratus was a man of Ephesus who in 356 BCE set fire to the Temple of Artemis, traditionally on the night Alexander the Great was born, in order to win lasting fame.
Phocion was an Athenian statesman and general, elected general forty-five times, known for his austere honesty.
Pytheas was a Greek navigator and geographer from Massalia, modern Marseille, who made a voyage to north-western Europe around 325 BCE.
Sun Bin was a Chinese military strategist of the Warring States period, said to be a descendant of Sun Wu, author of The Art of War.
Ambhi was the king of Taxila in north-western India in the late 4th century BCE, known to the Greeks as Taxiles and also as Omphis.
Archidamus III was king of Sparta from about 360 to 338 BCE, son of Agesilaus II.
King Wuling of Zhao ruled the state of Zhao in northern China from 325 to 299 BCE.
Nectanebo I was the founder of the Thirtieth Dynasty, the last native dynasty of Egypt, reigning from 380 to 362 BCE.
Nectanebo II was the last native king of ancient Egypt, of the Thirtieth Dynasty.
Zopyrion was a Macedonian general whom Alexander the Great left as governor of Thrace.
